text:
A.9 Prediction performance and internal validation

Multiple imputation-pooled bootstrap optimism-correction (primary analysis)
Per the plan (A.9), the bootstrap optimism-correction is combined with multiple imputation by repeating the full bootstrap procedure within each of the 20 imputed datasets separately. The resulting optimism-corrected estimates from each imputed dataset are then pooled across imputations using Rubin’s rules, so that imputation uncertainty is reflected in the reported standard error.
We illustrate this for Harrell’s C-index, the calibration slope, the explained-variation measure (Nagelkerke’s pseudo-R^2 for Cox models), the time-dependent AUC, Brier score and Index of Prediction Accuracy summary, all using the non-time-varying model specification. Pooling proceeds the same way throughout: the full bootstrap (or bootstrap-cross-validation) procedure is repeated within each of the 20 imputed datasets, and the resulting estimates are combined across imputations using Rubin’s rules.
Why the non-time-varying model is used for all performance measures. The C-index, the calibration slope and the explained-variation measure summarise how well a single risk score per patient (the linear predictor) ranks and calibrates patients. With a time-varying effect of ER, the patients’ ranking changes over follow-up, so no single risk score exists. For the time-dependent AUC, Brier score and Index of Prediction Accuracy we use the same model, so that all performance measures describe the same model. 
Likely consequences. The constant ER effect is an average over follow-up, and the proportional hazards assumption is violated for ER (A.8). Therefore, the model whose performance is reported here differs from the final model in A.5 (Table 2) including the time-varying ER term and is probably somewhat less accurate. Discrimination and calibration may thus be slightly mis-estimated, in particular for predictions early or late in follow-up. Because only one of the five predictors is affected, we would expect the differences to be small.  The results should be read as approximate.


Code
# Bootstrap optimism-correction for Harrell's C-index, the calibration
# slope, and the explained-variation measure (Nagelkerke's pseudo-R^2 for
# Cox models), repeated within each imputed dataset and pooled across
# imputations with Rubin's rules. The calibration-slope and R^2
# replicates reuse the same bootstrap-fitted model as the C-index
# replicate (fit_b):
# - slope_test is the coefficient obtained from refitting Surv ~ lp on
#   the original data using fit_b's linear predictor (Steyerberg-style
#   calibration slope); a value < 1 indicates overfitting.
# - r2_test is Nagelkerke's R^2 (Nagelkerke, 1991), computed from the
#   partial log-likelihood of fit_b's linear predictor evaluated on the
#   original data (via a zero-free-parameter, offset-only Cox model),
#   relative to the null-model log-likelihood on the original data. This
#   is the same explained-variation quantity reported by rms::validate()
#   (row "R2"); it is rebuilt here by hand, rather than taken from
#   rms::validate(), so that the per-replicate values needed for
#   Rubin's-rules pooling are accessible.
nagelkerke_r2 <- function(loglik_model, loglik_null, n) {
  LR    <- 2 * (loglik_model - loglik_null)
  R2_cs <- 1 - exp(-LR / n)
  R2_cs / (1 - exp(2 * loglik_null / n))
}

boot_optimism_C <- function(data, B = 100) {
  form  <- Surv(days, rezs) ~ PMP22_f + pT_num + pN_f + G_num + ER_f
  fit0  <- coxph(form, data = data, x = TRUE)
  c_app <- concordance(fit0)$concordance

  n <- nrow(data)
  null_orig     <- coxph(Surv(days, rezs) ~ 1, data = data)
  loglik_null_o <- null_orig$loglik[1]
  r2_app        <- nagelkerke_r2(fit0$loglik[2], loglik_null_o, n)

  c_train <- numeric(B); c_test <- numeric(B); slope_test <- numeric(B)
  r2_train <- numeric(B); r2_test <- numeric(B)
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    boot_data <- data[sample(seq_len(n), n, replace = TRUE), ]
    fit_b <- tryCatch(coxph(form, data = boot_data, x = TRUE),
                       error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(fit_b)) {
      c_train[b] <- NA; c_test[b] <- NA; slope_test[b] <- NA
      r2_train[b] <- NA; r2_test[b] <- NA
      next
    }
    c_train[b] <- concordance(fit_b)$concordance
    lp_orig   <- predict(fit_b, newdata = data, type = "lp")
    # NOTE: concordance()'s formula method assumes, by default, that LARGER
    # x means LONGER survival (opposite convention to a coxph risk score,
    # where larger lp means shorter survival) -- reverse = TRUE is required
    # here, or the resulting "concordance" is 1 minus the true value.
    c_test[b] <- concordance(Surv(data$days, data$rezs) ~ lp_orig,
                              reverse = TRUE)$concordance
    slope_fit <- tryCatch(coxph(Surv(data$days, data$rezs) ~ lp_orig),
                           error = function(e) NULL)
    slope_test[b] <- if (is.null(slope_fit)) NA else coef(slope_fit)[1]

    null_b <- tryCatch(coxph(Surv(days, rezs) ~ 1, data = boot_data),
                        error = function(e) NULL)
    r2_train[b] <- if (is.null(null_b)) NA else
      nagelkerke_r2(fit_b$loglik[2], null_b$loglik[1], n)
    test_fit <- tryCatch(coxph(Surv(data$days, data$rezs) ~ offset(lp_orig)),
                          error = function(e) NULL)
    r2_test[b] <- if (is.null(test_fit)) NA else
      nagelkerke_r2(test_fit$loglik[1], loglik_null_o, n)
  }
  optimism_C  <- mean(c_train - c_test, na.rm = TRUE)
  optimism_R2 <- mean(r2_train - r2_test, na.rm = TRUE)
  # The apparent calibration slope of a model against its own training data
  # is 1 by construction (lp already solves the partial-likelihood score
  # equations), so optimism = 1 - mean(slope_test) and the corrected slope
  # is simply mean(slope_test).
  list(apparent = c_app, corrected = c_app - optimism_C,
       boot_var = var(c_test, na.rm = TRUE),
       slope_corrected = mean(slope_test, na.rm = TRUE),
       slope_var = var(slope_test, na.rm = TRUE),
       R2_apparent = r2_app, R2_corrected = r2_app - optimism_R2,
       R2_var = var(r2_test, na.rm = TRUE))
}

Apparent discrimination (fit to the same data used to estimate the model) overstates true predictive ability. The pooled, optimism-corrected C-index above is the more honest number to report. The optimism-corrected calibration slope (0.88, i.e., somewhat below the ideal value of 1) indicates mild overfitting/optimism, plausible given the modest number of events relative to the number of parameters. Shrinking new predictions by this factor before use would be a reasonable. The pooled, optimism-corrected explained variation (0.1, Nagelkerke’s pseudo-R2 for Cox models) summarises the proportion of variation in disease-free survival accounted for by the model.

Time-dependent AUC, Brier score and Index of Prediction Accuracy (multiple imputation-pooled)
The time-dependent AUC, Brier score and Index of Prediction Accuracy are pooled the same way: the bootstrap-cross-validated riskRegression::Score() call is repeated within each of the 20 imputed datasets, and the resulting AUC(t) and Brier(t) estimates (together with their bootstrap-cross-validation standard errors) are combined across imputations using Rubin’s rules.


Code
set.seed(20260827)
mi_score_results <- vector("list", m_imp)
for (i in seq_len(m_imp)) {
  d_i <- complete(imp, i)
  d_i$PMP22_f <- factor(as.character(d_i$PMP22), levels = c("0", "1"),
                         labels = c("low", "high"))
  d_i$pN_f    <- factor(as.character(d_i$pN), levels = c("0", "1"),
                         labels = c("node-negative", "node-positive"))
  d_i$ER_f    <- factor(as.character(d_i$ER), levels = c("0", "1"),
                         labels = c("negative", "positive"))

  # standard (non-time-varying) model, as for the C-index, calibration slope and R^2
  fit_i <- coxph(Surv(days, rezs) ~ PMP22_f + pT + pN_f + G + ER_f,
                  data = d_i, x = TRUE, y = TRUE)

  sc_i <- Score(list("Full model" = fit_i),
                formula = Surv(days, rezs) ~ 1,
                data = d_i,
                times = c(365, 3 * 365, 5 * 365),
                metrics = c("auc", "brier"),
                summary = "ipa",
                split.method = "bootcv", B = 100, M = 150,
                progress.bar = NULL)

  auc_i   <- sc_i$AUC$score[sc_i$AUC$score$model   == "Full model", ]
  brier_i <- sc_i$Brier$score[sc_i$Brier$score$model == "Full model", ]

  mi_score_results[[i]] <- list(auc = auc_i$AUC, auc_se = auc_i$se,
                                 brier = brier_i$Brier, brier_se = brier_i$se,
                                 ipa = brier_i$IPA)
}

rubin_pool <- function(est_mat, se_mat) {
  # est_mat, se_mat: m (imputations) x k (time horizons) matrices
  m <- nrow(est_mat)
  pooled_est  <- colMeans(est_mat)
  within_var  <- colMeans(se_mat^2)
  between_var <- apply(est_mat, 2, var)
  data.frame(estimate = pooled_est,
             se = sqrt(within_var + (1 + 1 / m) * between_var))
}

ipa_mat      <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mi_score_results, `[[`, "ipa"))

pooled_auc   <- rubin_pool(auc_mat, auc_se_mat)
pooled_brier <- rubin_pool(brier_mat, brier_se_mat)

# full Rubin's-rules combination (which needs a within-imputation

Interpreting the output: - AUC(t) is Uno’s time-dependent area under the ROC curve: for patients still at risk at time t, the probability that a patient who has the event by t was assigned a higher predicted risk than a patient who is event-free through t. It ranges from 0.5 (no discrimination, equivalent to chance) to 1 (perfect discrimination), on the same conceptual scale as Harrell’s C-index, but is evaluated separately at each fixed horizon (1, 3, 5 years here) rather than averaged over the whole follow-up. - The Brier score is the time-dependent mean squared error between observed event status and predicted event probability at t. It reflects both discrimination and calibration jointly and ranges from 0 (perfect prediction) up to about 0.25 for an uninformative model at a 50% event rate, with lower values indicating better overall accuracy. - The Index of Prediction Accuracy (IPA) rescales the Brier score relative to a reference model without covariates (the marginal Kaplan-Meier estimate). IPA = 1 is perfect prediction, IPA = 0 means the model is no better than the covariate-free reference, and negative values mean the model performs worse than that reference. The Full model estimates reported by Score() above are already bootstrap-cross-validation corrected for optimism (split.method = "bootcv"), analogous to the optimism-correction applied to the C-index and calibration slope earlier.
As expected, AUC(t) decreases with a longer prediction horizon (1 year higher than 5 years) as predicting recurrence further into the future is intrinsically harder, since more competing/intervening information could in principle become available and the risk set composition changes. AUC(t) is somewhat higher than the (time-averaged) C-index above, which is an expected pattern. The two target related but distinct estimands (Uno-type time-dependent AUC at a fixed horizon vs. Harrell’s C averaged across all comparable pairs over the entire follow-up) and are not expected to numerically coincide. The pattern is broadly similar to the multiple imputation-pooled AUC(t), Brier score and IPA reported above. The complete-case and multiple imputation-pooled estimates are not expected to coincide exactly, given the different analysis populations (208 complete cases here vs. all 248 patients) and the different treatment of missing data.

A.11 Reporting

To highlight how this pre-specified analysis plan would read once written up for a clinical journal, this subsection presents a concise, self-contained results write-up.






Illustrative results write-up, as in a published paper






Methods (brief). In a retrospective multicentre cohort of women with primary breast cancer (Tong et al. 2010), PMP22 gene expression and four established clinical factors (tumour size (pT), nodal status (pN), tumour grade (G) and estrogen receptor status (ER)) were evaluated as predictors of disease-free survival (DFS). All five predictors were specified a priori on clinical grounds; none was added or dropped based on its own association with outcome. The primary analysis fitted a multivariable Cox proportional-hazards model with all five predictors entered simultaneously, with missing predictor values handled by multiple imputation (20 imputed datasets, multivariate imputation by chained equations) and estimates combined with Rubin’s rules. Because the proportional- hazards assumption was violated for ER (scaled Schoenfeld residuals), a pre-specified ER x log(follow-up time) interaction term was included to let the ER effect vary over follow-up. A complete-case analysis served as a sensitivity check. Model performance was assessed for the corresponding model without the ER x log(follow-up time) term (constant ER effect) and summarised by Harrell’s C-index, a bootstrap-based calibration slope, Nagelkerke’s explained-variation measure (pseudo-R2), and time-dependent AUC, Brier score and Index of Prediction Accuracy (IPA) at 1, 3 and 5 years, each corrected for optimism by bootstrap resampling repeated within every imputed dataset.


Patients
Of 249 patients in the original cohort, 248 were available in the public analysis dataset. Of these, 208 (84%) had complete data on all five predictors and were additionally used for complete-case sensitivity analyses; the remaining 40 patients (16%) had at least one missing predictor and were included, via multiple imputation, in the primary analysis population of all 248 patients (Figure 1). Over a median potential follow-up of 8.9 years (reverse Kaplan-Meier estimate), 109 (44%) of 248 patients experienced disease recurrence or death.

Overview
The workflow below is deliberately built to reproduce mistakes that are routinely seen in applied practice. It screens each candidate predictor’s univariable ( marginal) association with the outcome, keeps only variables that pass a significance filter, and treats the resulting reduced model as if it had been pre-specified.

B.1 Univariable screening
Each predictor is tested on its own, using whatever cases happen to be non-missing for that single variable. Therefore, the sample size silently differs from test to test, a detail that is rarely reported in practice.

  fit <- coxph(form, data = d)
  s <- summary(fit)
  data.frame(variable = v, n = nrow(d),
             HR = round(s$coefficients[, "exp(coef)"], 2),
             p_value = s$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"])  # full precision; used for the screen below
}))

B.2 Apply a significance filter
Here we will use 0.05 as significance criterion.

selected <- uni_results$variable[uni_results$p_value < alpha_screen]

Dropped (including, notably, PMP22 — the variable of primary interest): PMP22, pT, G 


PMP22 (p = 0.978) and G are dropped outright, and pT (p = 0.061) narrowly misses the threshold too. The screen never gives PMP22 a chance to be assessed jointly with the clinical factors; exactly the assessment the study was designed to make. This happens because PMP22’s univariable association with disease-free survival is masked by its correlation with ER. Only conditional on ER (and the other factors) does PMP22’s prognostic value emerge.

B.4 Missing data
No missing-data mechanism is examined. Each stage above uses whichever complete cases happen to be available for the variables involved at that stage (247/248 at the univariable stage for PMP22 and ER, 230 for pT, 219 for pN, 227 for G; 218 for the final reduced model). These inconsistent sample sizes that are easy to lose track of and rarely reconciled in reports built this way.

B.5 Interactions and assumptions — not checked
In a workflow like this, interaction terms and modeling assumptions (proportional hazards, functional form, influential points) are typically not examined once a “final” reduced model has been reached. We deliberately do not run them here either, to reflect this common practice. Part A shows what they would have revealed. (Notably, the ER proportional-hazards violation, which affects conclusions about PMP22 specifically.)

B.6 Reporting
The coefficients, hazard ratios, confidence intervals and p-values from fit_b_step would typically be reported as if pN and ER had been the pre-specified variables of interest, with language such as “independent prognostic factors,” and with no acknowledgment that they were chosen because of, not despite, their own association with the outcome. The resulting standard errors and p-values do not account for the selection process and are anti-conservative.
